newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade negotiators with China to leave jobs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade negotiators with China to leave jobs.

text.p: The top two U.S. trade negotiators with China announced on Tuesday plans to leave the government, creating a gap in talks on Beijing's World Trade Organisation bid that will be hard to fill, analysts said.
A U.S. Trade Representative spokesman said Assistant Trade Representative Lee Sands, who had been leading U.S. talks with China on its WTO bid, and Deborah Lehr, his deputy, planned to leave in June.

The agency confirmed the resignation plans after the Washington Post reported Tuesday that the two were talking to former Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor about joining his law firm to represent U.S. companies seeking access to China and other Asian markets.
USTR spokesman Jay Ziegler said "any employee in government can resign and seek another job" and the trade representative's office was working on a "smooth transition."
"It would be a great mistake to read into this a change in policy with regard to WTO negotiations," Ziegler said.

He said Robert Cassidy, assistant trade representative for Asia and Pacific affairs since 1992, will take over the China portfolio. Cassidy has been with the USTR since 1986, when he became deputy assistant for industry affairs. Before that he served in the U.S. Treasury's international division.
Trade analysts said Sands, who worked at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing for 10 years, and Lehr would be sorely missed.
"It's a huge hole," said Greg Mastel, a China trade expert with the Economic Strategy Institute think tank.
"This transition will make it much less likely that talks will conclude this year," said Jeffrey Schott, trade analyst with the Institute for International Economics.

"There was an outside chance that the talks could have been completed this year but that was becoming increasingly iffy given the political debate here in Washington," Schott said. "This means the issue will spill well over into 1998."

Reports of possible efforts by China to influence the 1996 elections through illegal campaign contributions has raised concerns in Congress about Beijing's WTO bid and made it more difficult politically for the administration to push for China on trade issues and resist lawmakers' efforts to have a bigger say in U.S. policy on Beijing's WTO bid, analysts said.

"The political consensus in the United States that might have allowed it (China's WTO bid) to happen has really eroded in recent weeks," Mastel said. "I just don't think the Clinton administration is going to want to push for China's WTO membership under these circumstances."

Kenneth DeWoskin, a China expert at University of Michigan, said it may be years before China wins entry into the WTO. He said China had made some concessions in trade on manufactured goods but had yielded little on services industries, which would help most in reducing the huge U.S. trade deficit with China.
